**Ch 040 Draft — Check**

The draft is a dramatic monologue / soliloquy. The compression is heavy internally. Let me trace each potential problem.

**"'Twas not so hard a task. Oh, hard! that to fire others, the match itself must needs be wasting!"**

In the source, the passage reads: *"'Twas not so hard a task. I thought to find one stubborn, at the least; but my one cogged circle fits into all their various wheels, and they revolve. Or, if you will, like so many ant-hills of powder, they all stand before me; and I their match. Oh, hard! that to fire others, the match itself must needs be wasting!"*

The source establishes the "match" metaphor (Ahab as the match, the crew as gunpowder ant-hills) before the "Oh, hard!" exclamation. The draft cuts the entire "cogged circle / ant-hills of powder / I their match" passage and jumps directly to "Oh, hard! that to fire others, the match itself must needs be wasting!" — leaving "the match itself" without any local antecedent. A reader who has not seen the source encounters: *'Twas not so hard a task. Oh, hard! that to fire others, the match itself must needs be wasting!* The word "match" arrives without the simile that gave it meaning. The two halves of the pivot are also broken: "not so hard" is supposed to contrast with the crew's easy yielding, and "Oh, hard!" is the ironic cost of being the igniting agent. Without the intervening simile, "the match itself" is an unglossed metaphor and "Oh, hard!" reads as contradicting "not so hard" with no logical bridge.

This is a **broken_pivot / missing_gloss** combined failure: the connective pivot from "'Twas not so hard" → crew-as-powder → Ahab-as-match → "Oh, hard!" is structurally severed, and "the match itself" has no definitional antecedent in the draft. A competent reader would be genuinely confused by what "the match itself" refers to.

**"Swerve me? The path to my fixed purpose is laid with iron rails..."**

In the source, the "Swerve me?" challenge is preceded by an extended address to the gods ("ye cricket-players, ye pugilists, ye deaf Burkes and blinded Bendigoes!... Come, Ahab's compliments to ye; come and see if ye can swerve me. Swerve me?"). The draft cuts all of this and opens cold with "Swerve me?" This is an **unattributed/broken pivot**: the challenge "Swerve me?" is a reply/retort to an imagined interlocutor who was set up in the cut passage. However, the sentence "Swerve me? The path to my fixed purpose..." is Ahab's rhetorical self-answer; the antecedent "ye" (the gods being addressed) was established in the immediately preceding lines of the same monologue. Because this is a soliloquy where Ahab's addressee shifts throughout, and because a competent reader can infer from context that Ahab is challenging some imagined opposition (gods, fate), the gate test suggests this is a less-ornamented version rather than a genuinely confusing one. **Not a valid finding.**
